title: How Members Represent
short: Members may act as delegates (vote as constituents want), trustees (use their own judgment) or politicos (mix the two); divided government, partisanship and the pull of reelection shape their choices.
trouble: Students think one role is the correct one. Each has a defense: delegates follow the people's wishes; trustees bring judgment and information. Most members blend them.

blocks.html: Each member of the House or Senate answers to voters back home, to a party, and to a conscience. How should a member decide? Political scientists describe three roles.

doc.title: Edmund Burke to the electors of Bristol, 1774
doc.source: Speech at the conclusion of the poll, November 1774 (The Works of Edmund Burke, vol. 2)
paras: But his unbiased opinion, his mature judgment, his enlightened conscience, he ought not to sacrifice to you, to any man, or to any set of men living.

marks.text: he ought not to sacrifice to you
marks.note: The classic statement of the trustee view: the member owes voters his judgment, not only his work.

blocks.html: Each role has a real defense, and each fits the Constitution's mixed design. The House, with two-year terms, pulls members toward the delegate role; the Senate's six-year terms give more room to act as trustees. Other forces shape the choice: party leaders and voters who expect party loyalty; divided government, when one party holds the presidency and another a house of Congress; and the pull of reelection. Incumbents are hard to beat: House members who run again have won more than 90 percent of the time in most elections since the 1980s, helped by name recognition and constituent service ("casework"). Madison argued in Federalist No. 57 that frequent elections and living under their own laws would keep representatives faithful.
Members may act as delegates (vote as constituents want), trustees (use their own judgment) or politicos (mix the two). Party, divided government and reelection shape their choices.

blocks.title: Name the role
blocks.q: A senator's state strongly supports a bill; after studying it she votes no, saying it will hurt the country, and explains her reasons at home.
steps: She follows her own judgment over constituents' wishes.

blocks.title: Mixed cases
blocks.q: A House member always votes with farmers in his district on farm bills but follows his own judgment on foreign policy, which few constituents follow closely. Which role?
steps: On one issue he acts as a delegate, on another as a trustee.

blocks.html: Thinking one role is the correct one. Each has defenders: delegates follow the people's wishes; trustees bring judgment and information. Most members blend them. Practice asks you to identify the role in an example, never to rank them.
